html:
The Iliad is an ancient Greek epic poem about the Trojan War, put into the form we know in about the 8th century BCE and credited to Homer. With its companion, the Odyssey, it is the oldest work of European literature that people still read for pleasure.

It does not tell the whole war. It covers a few weeks in its tenth year, when Achilles, the best Greek fighter, quarrels with the commander Agamemnon and refuses to fight. His friend Patroclus is killed, Achilles returns in fury and kills the Trojan prince Hector, and the poem ends with Hector's father Priam begging for his son's body.

  • 24 books, about 15,700 lines, in dactylic hexameter, the long six beat line of Greek epic.
  • It grew out of a long tradition of oral poetry. Its stock phrases ("swift footed Achilles", "rosy fingered dawn") helped singers compose as they performed.
  • Its memory of rich kings and bronze armour reaches back to Mycenaean Greece, centuries before it was written down.

Writing it down was possible because the Greeks had just adapted the Phoenician alphabet into the Greek alphabet. The poem then became the shared schoolbook of the Greek world. Children learned to read from it, Alexander the Great is said to have slept with a copy, and Roman poets answered it, most famously Virgil in the Aeneid.
